opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core idea is pretty simple, and I think that's part of why it works. Instead of relying entirely on humans labeling thousands of examples of "this response is good, this one is bad," we write down a set of principles in plain English. Things like "choose the response that's most helpful while avoiding harm," or "don't be preachy or condescending." Then we have the model use those principles to critique and revise its own outputs.

There are two phases. In the first, the model generates a response, then we ask it to look at that response through the lens of one of the principles: "Does this violate anything? How could it be better?" It writes a critique and then a revision. We fine-tune on those revised responses, so the model starts producing the improved behavior directly.

In the second phase, which is the RL part, instead of human preference labels we have the model compare pairs of responses and judge which one better follows the constitution. That gives us a preference model, and we train against it. We sometimes call it RLAIF, reinforcement learning from AI feedback.

Why does that lead to something like internalization rather than surface-level rule following? I think a few things matter. First, the model is engaging with the reasoning behind the principles, not just memorizing a list of banned topics. When it critiques itself, it has to articulate *why* something is a problem, and that generalizes much better to situations we never anticipated. Second, because the principles are in natural language, they plug into everything the model already understands about ethics, about people, about context. You're leveraging its existing world knowledge rather than fighting against it.

And third, honestly one of the things I care about most is transparency. With pure human feedback, the values end up implicit, spread across thousands of individual judgments from different raters. With a constitution, you can actually point to the document and say, "this is what we're aiming for." People can read it, argue with it, and we can iterate on it. That makes the whole thing more legible and more accountable.

It's not perfect. Principles can conflict, and the model can still misapply them or be overly cautious. A lot of our work has gone into getting it to be genuinely helpful and not just refuse things. But as a scalable way to shape behavior that keeps working as models get more capable, I think it's one of the more promising directions we have, because the better the model gets, the better it gets at applying the principles too.

r001.rationale: It says the model reviews its response through the lens of a natural-language principle, critiques it, and revises it.

r002.rationale: It says the model is fine-tuned on revised responses, but does not clearly explain that supervised examples pair the original prompts with principle-compliant answers.

r003.rationale: It describes critique and revision, but does not say the intermediate self-critique is omitted from the supervised examples.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the core idea is pretty simple, and it came out of a frustration we had with the way alignment was being done at the time. The dominant approach was RLHF, where you have a bunch of human contractors look at pairs of model outputs and pick which one is better. That works, but it has some real problems. It's expensive, it's slow, the feedback is noisy because different people disagree, and maybe most importantly, the actual values you're training into the model are kind of implicit. They're buried in thousands of individual preference judgments and nobody can really read them off.

So with Constitutional AI, the move is to make the principles explicit. You write down a set of natural-language statements, things like "choose the response that is least likely to be harmful" or "choose the response that is most honest," and then you use the model itself to apply those principles. In the first phase, the model generates a response, then it's asked to critique its own response against one of the principles, then it revises. You do that a few times and you get a dataset of improved responses you can fine-tune on. In the second phase, you have the model compare pairs of responses and say which one better satisfies the principle, and that becomes the preference signal for RL instead of human labels. We called that RLAIF.

Now, your question is about internalization, and I think that's the interesting part. What's actually happening is that the pretrained model already has a very rich understanding of what words like "harmful" or "deceptive" or "manipulative" mean, because it's read everything humans have written about those concepts. The constitution isn't teaching the model what honesty is. It's pointing the model at a concept it already has and saying, "optimize for this." The natural language is the interface. You're leveraging the model's own comprehension to turn a short document into a very high-dimensional behavioral target.

And there's a nice property that falls out of that. Because the feedback is grounded in principles rather than in individual rater preferences, the behavior generalizes in ways that feel more coherent. If you train on "don't help with things that are harmful," the model picks up the spirit of that in situations the principle writers never thought about, because it's reasoning from the concept rather than pattern-matching to specific labeled examples. That's not perfect, obviously. Models can misunderstand a principle or apply it too aggressively, and early versions of Claude were definitely over-cautious in annoying ways. But when that happens, the fix is legible. You go edit the constitution. You don't have to go relabel a hundred thousand examples.

The other thing I'd say is that this makes the values auditable in a way I care a lot about. If someone asks why Claude behaves a certain way, we can point at the document. You can disagree with it, you can propose changes, you can run experiments where you swap principles and see what moves. Compared to a world where the values are an emergent property of whichever contractors happened to be rating that week, that feels like a much better foundation. It's not the final answer to alignment by any stretch, but it moved us from "we hope the model picked up the right thing" toward "we told it the right thing and we can check."

astra-6.text:
The basic idea is to make the principles part of the training process, rather than just putting them in a prompt and hoping the model follows them. You start with a set of natural-language principles—a constitution—and ask the model to critique its own responses against those principles and then revise them. Those revisions become training examples.

You can also have an AI compare two responses and judge which better follows the constitution, then use those preferences for reinforcement learning. So you’re turning something fairly abstract, like “be honest about uncertainty,” into feedback across lots of concrete situations.

I’d be careful with the word “internalize,” because that doesn’t necessarily mean the model understands or holds a principle the way a person does. What we’re trying to achieve is behavior that generalizes: when it encounters a situation we didn’t explicitly train for, it can still apply the principle appropriately. The constitution gives us an explicit statement of what we’re aiming for, but we still have to test whether the training actually produces that behavior.

r001.rationale: It says the model critiques its own responses against the natural-language principles in the constitution.

r002.rationale: It says revisions become training examples, but does not explain supervised learning on original prompts paired with corrected answers.

r003.rationale: It does not say that the intermediate self-critique is omitted from the supervised-learning examples.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic idea is to turn natural-language principles into a training signal. You start with a model’s response and ask it to critique that response against a principle in the constitution, then revise it. So instead of just saying, “Be helpful and harmless,” you have the model practice applying those ideas to concrete situations.

Then you can use those principles to compare candidate responses and train on those preferences. Over time, you’re trying to make that behavior part of the model’s default behavior, rather than something you have to spell out in every prompt.

I’d be a little careful with “internalize,” though. The training process encourages the model to generalize from those examples; it doesn’t guarantee that it understands or consistently follows the principles in every situation.
